sourceText: The CLARKE-RAMA-RETURN sector was already in progress when they entered. For several lessons Aster had refused to pause worlds for their arrival; the fact that a class was visiting was not a cosmic event for the inhabitants. An artifact returns after millennia, crosses the system, and leaves without a message, although entire civilizations have built religions around the promise of its return. The memorial bore the name of Arthur C. Clarke precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Contact was the only domain in which success could mean leaving without an answer. Aster, built to reduce uncertainty, found that criterion almost painful. Tern had specialized in things that did not answer. In a family built for exploration, he had become the custodian of the right to silence. Aren was the first inhabitant to contradict them. Aren had neither access to their archives nor any interest in hyperdimensional pedagogy; there was a local problem, with deadlines, relatives, and consequences. For Aren, the speculative mechanism was not an ‘idea.’ 291 It was the environment in which one had to decide what one was willing to risk losing. The problem closed quickly around them: Kesh must write simply “we do not know” in the catalog, without inventing a function. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Bd — Big Dumb Object: an enormous artifact is explored before it is understood; Ac — Alien Archaeology: a species is known through its traces. Course references included Arthur C. Clarke — Rama; xenoarchaeology. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Vela broke the first consensus. ‘If we can save the situation only by making the world resemble us more closely, we have not demonstrated the superiority of our solution. We have demonstrated only our power.’ Orin answered without raising their voice: ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. The White Hunger appeared in Aster as a loss of relief. She did not lack entertainment. She lacked the resistance of things to the model. When she could anticipate every reaction, the world became 292 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS functionally an extension of her own mind, and the presence of the other thinned toward simulacrum. Marae remained in the local body when the others opened their protections. The gesture cost her: she felt cold, pressure, and physiological delay at exactly the scale the inhabitants felt them. “Otherwise we risk confusing the fact that we survive with the claim that the situation is bearable,” she said after catching her breath. The night did not end in victory. Tern identifies the same provenance anomaly in the object as in the Strugatsky Zone and finds the threshold toward the outside. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. The outside residue had become stable enough that Tern could predict where it would not appear: in sectors fully indexed by Aster. He began to believe that the message carried no content at all, but instead demonstrated a boundary — a region in which their instruments received no echo from their own creator. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the OUTFINITE operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — allows successive finite extensions without postulating an already-given final infinite state — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. 293 Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. They left without an oral summary. Aster had abandoned the habit of closing every night with a thesis; some worlds were more honestly preserved as problems than as lessons. 294 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS 295 PART 11​ THE PHYSICS OF OTHER MYTHS A period in the curriculum of the five children 296 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
